slides.title: The big idea
slides.html:
On a sphere, the "straight lines" are great circles, circles whose center is the sphere's center, like the equator and the lines of longitude. For two distinct nonantipodal points on a sphere, the shorter great-circle arc is the unique shortest surface path. Antipodal points have infinitely many shortest semicircles. A whole great circle is not itself a shortest path.

A triangle on a sphere can have three right angles: start at the North Pole, go down a longitude line to the equator, a quarter of the way around the equator, and back up. Its angle sum is 270 degrees. For a nondegenerate convex spherical triangle bounded by shorter great-circle arcs, the angle sum exceeds 180 degrees. A sphere model also differs from Euclidean incidence: antipodal points lie on infinitely many great circles. Any two great circles meet, so there are no parallel lines. Enrichment: a non-Euclidean geometry.

slides.title: Check yourself
slides.html: Why doesn't the 180 degree angle sum hold on a sphere?
slides.reveal: Its proof needs the Parallel Postulate, and on a sphere there are no parallel great circles.
